response.text:
gSASRec directly supports testing the objective before changing architecture. Its 2024 extended abstract recommends 128–256 negatives and calibration t=0.75; t=1 targets probability calibration but can slow convergence. For k uniform negatives, α=k/(catalogue_size−1), β=1−t+tα, and gBCE is [β·softplus(−s_positive)+Σ softplus(s_negative)]/(k+1). Preserve this weighting: averaging negatives separately changes the objective. The 2025 journal extension reports ranking and calibration improvements, but experiments cover MovieLens, Steam and Gowalla—not these four Amazon categories. [gBCE formulation and settings](https://www.ijcai.org/proceedings/2024/0939.pdf), [journal extension](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/336442/).

Multi-negative softmax is another credible baseline. RecSys 2025 eSASRec combines sampled softmax with LiGR layers and SASRec’s training task; its aggregate gains cannot establish the loss’s isolated contribution. A 2024 paper revised in 2025 compares BCE, categorical cross-entropy and BPR across five datasets/four models: full-catalogue categorical cross-entropy has the tightest ranking bounds, whereas sampled objectives behave differently; one-negative categorical cross-entropy equals BPR, and sampled BCE has the strongest worst-case bound. These findings do not establish a universal winning loss. [eSASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.06450), [loss comparison and code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.07770).

Practical inference: compare one-negative BCE, multi-negative BCE, gBCE and multi-negative softmax with architecture, splits and seeds fixed; report validation macro HR@10 and GPU cost. For nonuniform sampling, explicitly distinguish proposal-corrected softmax from uncorrected candidate discrimination. Weak training separation alone cannot diagnose generalization failure or prove calibration is the bottleneck.
